queries.text: Why does a single application of the variational (Temple-type) trial-state lower bound on the spectral gap to the tensor product of n non-interacting identical quartic (anharmonic) oscillators degrade with n and become negative at n = 5 copies, whereas certifying the one-body gap alone and using that the spectrum of a sum of commuting one-body Hamiltonians consists of sums of one-body eigenvalues gives a gap bound uniform in the number of copies?

Volume-uniform gap for decoupled degrees of freedom: a trial-state gap certificate applied globally to many identical quartic oscillators fails (negative bound at five copies) because the trial-state variance grows with the number of copies, while a per-factor certificate plus the spectral structure of a tensor sum of commuting one-body operators keeps the gap positive independent of the copy number.

Trial-state gap certificate on a product of identical quartic oscillators: global application gives a bound turning negative at five copies; single-factor certification followed by the spectrum of a sum of commuting one-body operators gives a positive, copy-number-independent bound. Why?

Why is a one-shot trial-state gap certificate not uniform in the number of decoupled identical quartic oscillator copies, going negative at five copies, and why does the factorized route - certify one factor, then use that eigenvalues of a sum of commuting one-body operators are sums of one-body eigenvalues - yield a spectral gap lower bound independent of the number of copies?
